summary: This document gives implementers guidelines for MPLS forwarding and a basis for evaluating forwarding implementations. It highlights practical requirements that are easy to overlook, or that are optional in the standards but are often treated as mandatory by network providers.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a checklist for building a mail-sorting machine, including things the official manual forgot but customers always expect. This RFC lists what MPLS equipment should really do when moving packets.

questions: what do providers expect from mpls routers
how do mpls routers handle small packets
subtitle: How to build and test MPLS routers that handle modern forwarding requirements.

tldr.problem: Network operators and equipment implementers often disagree on what MPLS forwarding features and performance levels are actually required. Standards documents leave many details optional or underspecified, even when providers treat them as mandatory.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7325 provides practical guidelines for MPLS forwarding, covering basics like label stacks and multipath load balancing, pseudowires, multicast, OAM, and performance with small packets. It includes a checklist of questions to ask suppliers and testing guidelines so implementers understand what operators really need.
tldr.outcome: Equipment suppliers and network operators can align expectations. Implementers know which optional features matter in practice, and operators have a standard way to evaluate if equipment meets their real requirements.

today: RFC 7325 is an Informational RFC published in August 2014. It remains essential guidance for understanding MPLS forwarding requirements and evaluating MPLS implementations. Service providers, network operators, and equipment vendors still use this document as a reference for what constitutes a complete and performant MPLS implementation. The combination of traffic engineering, pseudowire services, and multipath forwarding it describes continues to define how modern service provider networks operate.

sections.title: Forwarding Challenges and Misconceptions
sections.content: MPLS is a packet forwarding mechanism that uses short labels to identify forwarding paths and services. While MPLS is defined in standards like RFC 3031, many real-world requirements are left as optional or underspecified. This document addresses long-standing misconceptions and documents what network operators actually expect from MPLS implementations. For example, early MPLS implementations incorrectly assumed label stacks would always be shallow (one or two labels), but modern networks routinely use three, four, or more labels due to traffic engineering, VPNs, fast reroute, and hierarchical LSP tunneling. The document clarifies that label stacks can be arbitrarily deep and that forwarding engines must handle them. Another misconception: operators expect MPLS routers to handle arbitrary sequences of small packets at full line rate, because TCP acknowledgments and other control traffic often arrive in short bursts that can overwhelm forwarding engines with insufficient buffering.
sections.plainLanguage: The manual for MPLS did not say how deep a stack of labels could be, or how fast it had to handle tiny packets. Operators expect routers to handle both. This RFC explains what people really need.

sections.title: Core Forwarding Architecture
sections.content: MPLS defines a label as a short identifier (20 bits) used to look up a forwarding path in a label switching router (LSR). A router receiving an MPLS packet looks up the top label in an Incoming Label Map (ILM) to determine what to do: swap the label (replace the top label and forward to another LSR), pop the label (remove it and forward), or push a label (add one). When multiple labels exist in a stack, the bottom label has a special S bit (bit 0) set to 1 to mark the end of the stack. The Traffic Class (TC) field (formerly called EXP) carries Quality of Service information like DSCP. Modern MPLS also supports differentiated services where different LSPs map TC values to per-hop behaviors, and explicit congestion notification (ECN). The TTL field determines how many hops the packet can traverse, preventing infinite loops. Special-purpose labels (0-15) have reserved meanings: label 0 is IPv4 Explicit NULL, label 2 is IPv6 Explicit NULL, and label 1 is Router Alert. Labels 3-15 have been assigned for other purposes, and RFC 7274 extended the space with an additional registry for labels 16-1048575.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is like a ticket that says 'send this to the next station.' Labels can be replaced, removed, or added. The most basic ones are reserved for special purposes like 'watch this packet closely.'

sections.title: Multipath and Load Balancing
sections.content:
Modern networks use multipath (ECMP, link aggregation, or similar) to distribute traffic across multiple parallel links. For good load balancing, routers must examine fields in the packet to create a hash: the standard technique at each router is to examine the MPLS label stack and, if the payload is IP, examine IP addresses and port numbers. Without looking inside the MPLS labels to the IP header, traffic is poorly balanced, especially when carrying many small flows. Operators and providers treat multipath support as mandatory, not optional, for core networks.

When services like pseudowires and VPNs are carried over MPLS in networks with multipath, packet reordering can occur as traffic is distributed across parallel links. To prevent this, a pseudowire Control Word (CW) is used. The CW adds a framing header and includes a sequence number so the egress can detect and reorder out-of-order packets. For large flows (like a 1 Gb/s VPN on a network with 10 Gb/s links), a Flow Label or Entropy Label is added to improve hash distribution so a single large flow is not penalized by going to one path.

The MPLS Entropy Label (RFC 6790) is a newer approach where the ingress LSR adds an entropy label near the top of the stack, allowing core routers to use this pre-computed hash value instead of examining the entire stack and payload. This is essential for achieving forwarding performance in high-speed networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send all traffic to one path, it gets congested. Routers guess which path to use based on addresses. If the guess is bad, one path gets full and others are empty. Special labels help the router guess better.

sections.title: Packet Rates and Small-Packet Handling
sections.content:
A critical and often-overlooked requirement is the ability to forward small packets at line rate. TCP acknowledgments compressed in a connection can produce packets as small as 40-44 bytes of payload. On a 100 Gb/s Ethernet link, these packets arrive at a rate exceeding 150 million packets per second. Some operators and content providers specify that routers must sustain this rate, but the cost for very-high-speed interfaces is significant.

Alternatively, if a router cannot process small packets at full line rate, it MUST have sufficient on-chip buffering (before the packet decision engine) to absorb bursts of small packets and still maintain full forwarding rate for reasonable average packet sizes. Without this buffering, packets are randomly dropped before the QoS decision process, defeating Differentiated Services. With adequate buffering, packets are delivered to QoS queues where they can be handled according to policy rather than dropped randomly. A 4K packet buffer of 64-byte packets (256 KB) corresponds to only 20 microseconds of delay on a 100 Gb/s link, and the delay applies only when a burst of small packets occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny packets come very fast in short bursts. A router either has to be super fast, or have a waiting area so it does not drop them.

sections.title: Pseudowires, VPNs, and Advanced Services
sections.content: Pseudowires (PWs) emulate circuit services (like Frame Relay, ATM, or TDM) over packet networks by carrying the service payload inside MPLS tunnels. PWs add one or more labels to the stack and MAY use a Control Word for framing and sequence numbering. PWs are often carried inside VPN tunnels, adding yet another label. With fast reroute enabled, a network might have LDP over RSVP-TE tunnels carrying VPNs, producing label stacks of four or more labels. Multicast in MPLS is signaled with RSVP-TE (RFC 4875) for P2MP (point-to-multipoint) or LDP (RFC 6388) for both P2MP and MP2MP (multipoint-to-multipoint). At leaf nodes, MPLS pops the label and delivers the packet; at intermediate nodes, MPLS swaps; at bud nodes, both operations occur on the same packet. Multicast traffic replication can be complex to implement at high rates if the egress ports are congested. All of these services rely on the basic forwarding mechanics covered in earlier sections.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake wires and private networks add more labels. Sometimes a packet gets copied to many places. The router has to handle all these cases without dropping packets.

sections.title: OAM, DoS Protection, and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in MPLS includes continuity check and connectivity verification (CC-CV), loss measurement (LM), and delay measurement (DM). OAM packets are identified using the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) and associated channel headers. MPLS-TP (MPLS Transport Profile) extends these capabilities for carrier-grade services. Routers must support OAM packet processing while maintaining data forwarding performance. High OAM packet rates should be negotiated so the router is not overwhelmed.

DoS protection is critical when a router processes special-purpose labels or control packets. Unknown special-purpose labels should be rate-limited or dropped (not sent to a CPU at unlimited rate), and management protocols must be protected from being flooded. MPLS routers should separate data path and control path so that control traffic cannot be congested by data traffic.

The Time-to-Live (TTL) field provides basic loop prevention. Routers MUST decrement TTL for standard forwarding and also when using Fast Reroute bypass tunnels. Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP) can optimize hop-by-hop path verification in OAM.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to check if connections are working, measure how fast they are, and protect themselves from being flooded with junk. The TTL field stops packets from looping forever.
